questions.question: Which property defines a continuous random variable in this course?
options: It can take only finitely many isolated values
It must have a probability mass function giving positive mass to each value
A nonnegative density $f_X$ whose integrals give interval probabilities
It is always normally distributed

questions.question: What is $P(X=c)$ for a continuous random variable and a fixed real number $c$?
What can be said about the CDF of a continuous random variable?
options: It must be a step function
It is always constant
It is continuous
It is undefined outside the support

questions.question: Which example is naturally modeled as a continuous random variable?
options: The number of heads in ten coin tosses
The number of aces in a five-card hand
The number of calls arriving in a minute
The lifetime of a light bulb

questions.question: If $X$ is continuous, which expression represents $P(2\le X\le 5)$?
options: $\int_2^5 f_X(x)\,\mathrm{d}x$
$5-2$ without using a density

questions.question: Why do endpoints usually not matter for intervals of a continuous random variable?
options: Because densities are always zero at endpoints
Because all intervals have probability one
Because continuous variables cannot have endpoints
Because individual points have probability zero

questions.question: Why is a density value $f_X(c)$ not itself the probability $P(X=c)$?
options: The density is always an integer count
Point probabilities are zero; probabilities come from areas over intervals
The density value $f_X(c)$ is always less than one, as every probability must be
$P(X=c)$ equals one whenever $c$ lies inside the support of $X$

questions.question: Does a continuous random variable require its density to be continuous everywhere?
options: Yes, both the CDF and the density must be continuous everywhere on the real line
No, its CDF is continuous but the density need not be continuous everywhere
No, because the CDF must have jumps
Yes, because every density is constant

questions.question: Each function below is $0$ outside the stated intervals. Which one is a valid density of a continuous random variable?
Let $X\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)$, with density $1$ on $(0,1)$. Which statement about the value $0.5$ is correct?
options: $X=0.5$ cannot occur, since $\mathbb{P}(X=0.5)=0$
$\mathbb{P}(X=0.5)=0$, yet $0.5$ is as possible as any value
$\mathbb{P}(X=0.5)$ is undefined; only intervals get probabilities
